<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
Many bacteria are able to respire in the absence of oxygen by utilizing alternative electron acceptors. Due to the low redox potential of the nitrate/nitrite pair, nitrate is one of the preferred alternative electron acceptors. Bacterial anaerobic nitrate respiration can proceed along two different pathways. One pathway is the denitrification process, in which nitrate is sequentially reduced through nitrite, nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and finally to dinitrogen (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=DENITRIFICATION-PWY">nitrate reduction I (denitrification)</a>). In the second pathway, nitrate is first reduced to nitrite and the latter is subsequently converted in a six-electron reduction step to ammonia, which is secreted from the cell.
<p>
This six-electron reduction is catalyzed by the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NRFMULTI-CPLX">periplasmic nitrite reductase NrfAB</a>, a periplasmic complex made of several proteins. The catalytic subunit of this complex is <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=CYTOCHROMEC552-MONOMER">cytochrome <i>c</i><sub>552</sub> nitrite reductase</a>, a hexaheme <i>c</i>-type cytochrome encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=EG11781">nrfA</a> gene [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7309757">Liu81</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3002798">Kajie86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2833168">Liu88</a>].
The dissimilatory nitrite reductases are different from the assimilatory nitrite reductases in several ways, including their induction by nitrate under anaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4405508">Prakash73</a>] and the fact that they are not suppressed by the presence of ammonium [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5726295">vantRiet68</a>].
<p>
Four classes of nitrate reductases are known - a eukaryotic class, and three prokaryotic classes. The eukaryotic nitrate reductases are found in plants, algae and fungi, and are involved in assimilation of nitrate. They are composed of two identical subunits, and contain a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-8123">MoO<sub>2</sub>-molybdopterin cofactor</a> and an <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=FAD">FAD</a> prosthetic group. In general, plant enzymes prefer NADH as the electron donor (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADH-RXN">E.C. 1.7.1.1</a>) and fungal enzymes prefer NADPH (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPH-RXN">E.C. 1.7.1.3</a>), although some enzymes were reported
to accept either of these compounds (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPORNOPH-RXN">E.C. 1.7.1.2</a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14209328">Beevers64</a>].
Example for eukaryotic enzymes include the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=AT1G37130-MONOMER">assimilatory nitrate reductase (NADH)</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-3702"><i>Arabidopsis thaliana</i></a> and the
<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13438">assimilatory nitrate reductase (NADPH)</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-5141"><i>Neurospora crassa</i></a>. 
<p>
Prokaryotic nitrate reductases are divided into three classes, including a class of assimilatory enzymes and two classes of respiratory enzymes. All of them include a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-582">guanylyl molybdenum cofactor</a> cofactor, but differ in their substructures, cellular location, and cofactor requirement. Variabillity among enzymes is also found within the classes. Assimilatory prokaryotic nitrate reductases (NAS) are involved in the assimilation of nitrogen from nitrate for incorporation into protein. Despite their
relatedness, these enzymes vary in their substructures and cofactors. For example, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7499">assimilatory nitrate reductase [NAD(P)H]</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-290336"><i>Klebsiella michiganensis</i> M5al</a> is a heterodimer that utilizes NAD(P)H, while <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13441">ferredoxin--nitrate reductase</a> from the cyanobacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1140"><i>Synechococcus elongatus</i> PCC 7942 = FACHB-805</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13440">assimilatory nitrate reductase</a> from the Gram-negative bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-354"><i>Azotobacter vinelandii</i></a> are monomeric and utilize ferredoxin (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=1.7.7.2-RXN">E.C. 1.7.7.2</a>) and flavodoxin, respectively.
<p>
Respiratory nitrate reductases use nitrate as the electron acceptor of an anaerobic respiratory chain which
usually starts with the quinone pool (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=RXN0-6369">EC 1.7.99.4</a>).
One of these classes (NAR) consists of membrane-bound enzymes that are composed of three different subunits. These enzymes, which include <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7502">respiratory nitrate reductase</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-316"><i>Stutzerimonas stutzeri</i></a> and the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-83333"><i>Escherichia coli</i> K-12</a> enzymes <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NITRATREDUCTA-CPLX">nitrate reductase A</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NITRATREDUCTZ-CPLX">nitrate reductase Z</a>, are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane, with the active site facing the cytoplasm.
<p>
The second class of bacterial respiratory nitrate reductases (NAP) consists of periplasmic enzymes, which are usually heterodimers, although monomeric forms have been reported. Examples for enzymes belonging to this class include <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NAP-CPLX">periplasmic nitrate reductase</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-83333"><i>Escherichia coli</i> K-12</a> (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=RXN0-6369">EC 1.7.99.4</a>) and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7500">periplasmic nitrate reductase (cytochrome)</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-668"><i>Aliivibrio fischeri</i></a> (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=NITRATE-REDUCTASE-CYTOCHROME-RXN">EC 1.9.6.1</a>).
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
In the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> anaerobic respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase and nitrate reductase the transfer of electrons from NADH to nitrate is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force (H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> = 3) across the cytoplasmic membrane ([<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4385809">Cole68a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5996">Garland75</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/776172">Haddock75</a>] and see [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>]).
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 contains two NADH dehydrogenases - energy conserving NDH-I (shown in this pathway) and NDH-II which does not contribute to the proton gradient; both enzymes appear to be involved in anaerobic nitrate respiration [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7565112">Bongaerts95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9063459">Tran97</a>]. By analogy to the related enzyme from mitochondria, NDH-I is thought to function as a proton pump translocating 4H<sup>+</sup> per NADH oxidised (2e<sup>-</sup>) [H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> = 2] however a lower ratio of 3H<sup>+</sup>/2e<sup>-</sup> has also been proposed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8892824">Bogachev96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22392981">Wikstrom12</a>]. Nitrate induces the expression of the <i>nuo</i> operon (encoding NDH-I) in a NarL dependent manner [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7565112">Bongaerts95</a>]
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 also contains two energy conserving (H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> = 1) nitrate reductases. Expression of nitrate reductase A (NRA) occurs in response to high levels of nitrate in the environment whereas expression of nitrate reductase Z (NRZ) is not dependent on nitrate levels or anaerobiosis ([<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464201">Wang99e</a>] and see [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7747940">Bonnefoy94</a>]).
<p>
Quinones are the obligate redox carriers during anaerobic nitrate respiration; the concentration of menaquinone increases in cells grown anaerobically with nitrate while the concentration of ubiquinone decreases (as compared with cells grown aerobically) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/195602">Wallace77</a>]. Nitrate reductase A can use both menaquinol (shown in this pathway) and ubiquinol as electron donors [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2204318">Wissenbach90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1444716">Wissenbach92</a>]. In anaerobic growth with nitrate the major quinone is demethylmenaquinone (DMK) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2849923">Unden88</a>]; an <i>E. coli</i> strain containing only demethylmenaquinone is unable to grow with nitrate as terminal reductase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1444716">Wissenbach92</a>].
<p>

<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
Many bacteria are able to respire in the absence of oxygen by utilizing alternative electron acceptors. Due to the low redox potential of the nitrate/nitrite pair, nitrate is one of the preferred alternative electron acceptors. Bacterial anaerobic nitrate respiration can proceed along two different pathways. One pathway is the denitrification process, in which nitrate is sequentially reduced through nitrite, nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and finally to dinitrogen (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=DENITRIFICATION-PWY">nitrate reduction I (denitrification)</a>). In the second pathway, nitrate is first reduced to nitrite and the latter is subsequently converted in a six-electron reduction step to ammonia, which is secreted from the cell.
<p>
This six-electron reduction is catalyzed by the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NRFMULTI-CPLX">periplasmic nitrite reductase NrfAB</a>, a periplasmic complex made of several proteins. The catalytic subunit of this complex is <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=CYTOCHROMEC552-MONOMER">cytochrome <i>c</i><sub>552</sub> nitrite reductase</a>, a hexaheme <i>c</i>-type cytochrome encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=EG11781">nrfA</a> gene [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7309757">Liu81</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3002798">Kajie86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2833168">Liu88</a>].
The dissimilatory nitrite reductases are different from the assimilatory nitrite reductases in several ways, including their induction by nitrate under anaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4405508">Prakash73</a>] and the fact that they are not suppressed by the presence of ammonium [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5726295">vantRiet68</a>].
<p>
Four classes of nitrate reductases are known - a eukaryotic class, and three prokaryotic classes. The eukaryotic nitrate reductases are found in plants, algae and fungi, and are involved in assimilation of nitrate. They are composed of two identical subunits, and contain a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-8123">MoO<sub>2</sub>-molybdopterin cofactor</a> and an <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=FAD">FAD</a> prosthetic group. In general, plant enzymes prefer NADH as the electron donor (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADH-RXN">E.C. 1.7.1.1</a>) and fungal enzymes prefer NADPH (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPH-RXN">E.C. 1.7.1.3</a>), although some enzymes were reported
to accept either of these compounds (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPORNOPH-RXN">E.C. 1.7.1.2</a>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14209328">Beevers64</a>].
Example for eukaryotic enzymes include the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=AT1G37130-MONOMER">assimilatory nitrate reductase (NADH)</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-3702"><i>Arabidopsis thaliana</i></a> and the
<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13438">assimilatory nitrate reductase (NADPH)</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-5141"><i>Neurospora crassa</i></a>. 
<p>
Prokaryotic nitrate reductases are divided into three classes, including a class of assimilatory enzymes and two classes of respiratory enzymes. All of them include a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-582">guanylyl molybdenum cofactor</a> cofactor, but differ in their substructures, cellular location, and cofactor requirement. Variabillity among enzymes is also found within the classes. Assimilatory prokaryotic nitrate reductases (NAS) are involved in the assimilation of nitrogen from nitrate for incorporation into protein. Despite their
relatedness, these enzymes vary in their substructures and cofactors. For example, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7499">assimilatory nitrate reductase [NAD(P)H]</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-290336"><i>Klebsiella michiganensis</i> M5al</a> is a heterodimer that utilizes NAD(P)H, while <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13441">ferredoxin--nitrate reductase</a> from the cyanobacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1140"><i>Synechococcus elongatus</i> PCC 7942 = FACHB-805</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-13440">assimilatory nitrate reductase</a> from the Gram-negative bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-354"><i>Azotobacter vinelandii</i></a> are monomeric and utilize ferredoxin (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=1.7.7.2-RXN">E.C. 1.7.7.2</a>) and flavodoxin, respectively.
<p>
Respiratory nitrate reductases use nitrate as the electron acceptor of an anaerobic respiratory chain which
usually starts with the quinone pool (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=RXN0-6369">EC 1.7.99.4</a>).
One of these classes (NAR) consists of membrane-bound enzymes that are composed of three different subunits. These enzymes, which include <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7502">respiratory nitrate reductase</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-316"><i>Stutzerimonas stutzeri</i></a> and the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-83333"><i>Escherichia coli</i> K-12</a> enzymes <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NITRATREDUCTA-CPLX">nitrate reductase A</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NITRATREDUCTZ-CPLX">nitrate reductase Z</a>, are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane, with the active site facing the cytoplasm.
<p>
The second class of bacterial respiratory nitrate reductases (NAP) consists of periplasmic enzymes, which are usually heterodimers, although monomeric forms have been reported. Examples for enzymes belonging to this class include <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NAP-CPLX">periplasmic nitrate reductase</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-83333"><i>Escherichia coli</i> K-12</a> (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=RXN0-6369">EC 1.7.99.4</a>) and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-7500">periplasmic nitrate reductase (cytochrome)</a> from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-668"><i>Aliivibrio fischeri</i></a> (<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=REACTION&object=NITRATE-REDUCTASE-CYTOCHROME-RXN">EC 1.9.6.1</a>).
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
In the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> anaerobic respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase and nitrate reductase the transfer of electrons from NADH to nitrate is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force (H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> = 3) across the cytoplasmic membrane ([<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4385809">Cole68a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5996">Garland75</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/776172">Haddock75</a>] and see [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>]).
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 contains two NADH dehydrogenases - energy conserving NDH-I (shown in this pathway) and NDH-II which does not contribute to the proton gradient; both enzymes appear to be involved in anaerobic nitrate respiration [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7565112">Bongaerts95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9063459">Tran97</a>]. By analogy to the related enzyme from mitochondria, NDH-I is thought to function as a proton pump translocating 4H<sup>+</sup> per NADH oxidised (2e<sup>-</sup>) [H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> = 2] however a lower ratio of 3H<sup>+</sup>/2e<sup>-</sup> has also been proposed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8892824">Bogachev96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22392981">Wikstrom12</a>]. Nitrate induces the expression of the <i>nuo</i> operon (encoding NDH-I) in a NarL dependent manner [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7565112">Bongaerts95</a>]
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 also contains two energy conserving (H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> = 1) nitrate reductases. Expression of nitrate reductase A (NRA) occurs in response to high levels of nitrate in the environment whereas expression of nitrate reductase Z (NRZ) is not dependent on nitrate levels or anaerobiosis ([<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464201">Wang99e</a>] and see [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7747940">Bonnefoy94</a>]).
<p>
Quinones are the obligate redox carriers during anaerobic nitrate respiration; the concentration of menaquinone increases in cells grown anaerobically with nitrate while the concentration of ubiquinone decreases (as compared with cells grown aerobically) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/195602">Wallace77</a>]. Nitrate reductase A can use both menaquinol (shown in this pathway) and ubiquinol as electron donors [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2204318">Wissenbach90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1444716">Wissenbach92</a>]. In anaerobic growth with nitrate the major quinone is demethylmenaquinone (DMK) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2849923">Unden88</a>]; an <i>E. coli</i> strain containing only demethylmenaquinone is unable to grow with nitrate as terminal reductase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1444716">Wissenbach92</a>].
<p>

source_slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The <i>E. coli</i> K-12 genome encodes 3 quinol:oxygen oxidoreductases - <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CYT-O-UBIOX-CPLX">cytochrome <i>bo</i></a> (<i>cyoABCD</i>), cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I (<i>cydABX-cydH</i>) and <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=APP-UBIOX-CPLX">cytochrome <i>bd</i>-II</a> (<i>appCBX</i>). The three enzymes function as the major terminal oxidases in the aerobic respiratory chain of <i>E. coli</i>. Cytochrome <i>bo</i> is expressed when oxygen levels are high while cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I is expressed under oxygen limited conditions. Both enymes contribute to the generation of a proton motive force (PMF), cytochrome <i>bo</i> functions as a proton pump whilst cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I does not. Cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I catalyses ubiquinol oxidation with a H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> of 1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1850294">Puustinen91</a>]. The energetics of cytochrome <i>bd</i>-II are less clear; initial reports suggested that it did not contribute to PMF [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19542282">Bekker09</a>] while later work indicates that it generates PMF with an H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> of 0.94 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21987791">Borisov11a</a>].
<p>
Cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I catalyses the two electron oxidation of ubiquinol and the four electron reduction of oxygen to water. Oxidation of ubiquinol releases two protons into the periplasmic space and two electrons are transferred through the heme cofactors to the oxygen reducing site. Four protons are taken up from the cytoplasm for oxygen reduction (see review by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21756872">Borisov11</a>] and references within). The enzyme is a hetero-tetramer consisting of the CydAB core dimer [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3281937">Miller88b</a>] plus two accessory single transmembrane subunits, CydX and CydH [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31604309">Safarian19</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24681096">Hoeser14</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23749980">Vanorsdel13</a>].   
<p>
Cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I contains 3 bound hemes: heme <i>b<sub>558</sub></i>, heme <i>b<sub>595</sub></i> and heme <i>d</i>, present in a 1:1:1 ratio [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6307994">Miller83a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6321507">Kita84a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2856143">Miller86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2856144">Kita86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3040093">HataTanaka87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2549971">Rothery89</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2544229">Meinhardt89</a>]. Subunit I (CydA) contains all three heme cofactors and the periplasmically exposed quinol binding loop (Q loop); heme <i>b<sub>558</sub></i> acts as the primary electron acceptor and electrons are transferred to the heme <i>b<sub>595</sub></i> and heme <i>d</i> binuclear centre where oxygen is reduced to water [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8516338">Hill93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1851043">Newton91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31604309">Safarian19</a>]. 
<p>
Purified cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I has quinol peroxidase activity which may serve a detoxifying function <i>in vivo</I>; purified cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I does not show catalase activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27279363">AlAttar16</a>].   
<p>
Cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I supports respiration when <i>E. coli</i> encounters hydrogen sulfide (from the external environment or through the inadvertant degradation of cysteine); cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I (unlike cytochrome <i>bo</i>) is resistant to the inhibitory effects of hydrogen sulfide.  During aerobic growth in glycerol medium mutants lacking cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I cease growth upon addition of cystine to the culture medium, whereas mutants lacking cytochrome <i>bo</i> show only a modest reduction in growth; the &Delta;<i>cydAB</i> mutant defect is relieved in a &Delta;<i>tcyP</i> mutant indicating that the defect is a result of cystine import into the cytoplasm [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26991114">Korshunov16</a>] (see also [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27030302">Forte16</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33705279">Borisov21a</a>]).
<p>
Expression of <i>cydAB</i> is negatively regulated by <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PD00197">Fnr</a>, induced by anaerobiosis via the <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY0-1505">ArcA/ArcB two-component regulatory system</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2172211">Cotter90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9302022">Cotter97</a>], and repressed by H-NS under aerobic conditions, resulting in maximal expression under microaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8576043">Tseng96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11123679">Govantes00</a>].  Expression is induced by iron limitation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1478458">Cotter92</a>] and H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> exposure [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11016692">Lindqvist00</a>], and is sensitive to the level of DNA supercoiling [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11238966">Bebbington01</a>]. <i>cydAB</i> is upregulated when exposed to nitric oxide and cytochrome <i>bd</i>-1 confers resistance to nitric oxide stress when compared to cytochrome <i>bo</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19109594">Mason09</a>].
<p>
GFP-tagged cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I concentrates in mobile localised areas of the inner membrane of <i>E. coli</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19019148">Lenn08</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21756872">Borisov11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32924537">Borisov21</a>]</comment>

<comment datatype="string">The <i>E. coli</i> K-12 genome encodes 3 quinol:oxygen oxidoreductases - <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CYT-O-UBIOX-CPLX">cytochrome <i>bo</i></a> (<i>cyoABCD</i>), cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I (<i>cydABX-cydH</i>) and <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=APP-UBIOX-CPLX">cytochrome <i>bd</i>-II</a> (<i>appCBX</i>). The three enzymes function as the major terminal oxidases in the aerobic respiratory chain of <i>E. coli</i>. Cytochrome <i>bo</i> is expressed when oxygen levels are high while cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I is expressed under oxygen limited conditions. Both enymes contribute to the generation of a proton motive force (PMF), cytochrome <i>bo</i> functions as a proton pump whilst cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I does not. Cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I catalyses ubiquinol oxidation with a H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> of 1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1850294">Puustinen91</a>]. The energetics of cytochrome <i>bd</i>-II are less clear; initial reports suggested that it did not contribute to PMF [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19542282">Bekker09</a>] while later work indicates that it generates PMF with an H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> of 0.94 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21987791">Borisov11a</a>].
<p>
Cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I catalyses the two electron oxidation of ubiquinol and the four electron reduction of oxygen to water. Oxidation of ubiquinol releases two protons into the periplasmic space and two electrons are transferred through the heme cofactors to the oxygen reducing site. Four protons are taken up from the cytoplasm for oxygen reduction (see review by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21756872">Borisov11</a>] and references within). The enzyme is a hetero-tetramer consisting of the CydAB core dimer [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3281937">Miller88b</a>] plus two accessory single transmembrane subunits, CydX and CydH [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31604309">Safarian19</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24681096">Hoeser14</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23749980">Vanorsdel13</a>].   
<p>
Cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I contains 3 bound hemes: heme <i>b<sub>558</sub></i>, heme <i>b<sub>595</sub></i> and heme <i>d</i>, present in a 1:1:1 ratio [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6307994">Miller83a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6321507">Kita84a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2856143">Miller86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2856144">Kita86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3040093">HataTanaka87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2549971">Rothery89</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2544229">Meinhardt89</a>]. Subunit I (CydA) contains all three heme cofactors and the periplasmically exposed quinol binding loop (Q loop); heme <i>b<sub>558</sub></i> acts as the primary electron acceptor and electrons are transferred to the heme <i>b<sub>595</sub></i> and heme <i>d</i> binuclear centre where oxygen is reduced to water [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8516338">Hill93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1851043">Newton91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31604309">Safarian19</a>]. 
<p>
Purified cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I has quinol peroxidase activity which may serve a detoxifying function <i>in vivo</I>; purified cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I does not show catalase activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27279363">AlAttar16</a>].   
<p>
Cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I supports respiration when <i>E. coli</i> encounters hydrogen sulfide (from the external environment or through the inadvertant degradation of cysteine); cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I (unlike cytochrome <i>bo</i>) is resistant to the inhibitory effects of hydrogen sulfide.  During aerobic growth in glycerol medium mutants lacking cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I cease growth upon addition of cystine to the culture medium, whereas mutants lacking cytochrome <i>bo</i> show only a modest reduction in growth; the &Delta;<i>cydAB</i> mutant defect is relieved in a &Delta;<i>tcyP</i> mutant indicating that the defect is a result of cystine import into the cytoplasm [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26991114">Korshunov16</a>] (see also [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27030302">Forte16</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33705279">Borisov21a</a>]).
<p>
Expression of <i>cydAB</i> is negatively regulated by <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PD00197">Fnr</a>, induced by anaerobiosis via the <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY0-1505">ArcA/ArcB two-component regulatory system</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2172211">Cotter90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9302022">Cotter97</a>], and repressed by H-NS under aerobic conditions, resulting in maximal expression under microaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8576043">Tseng96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11123679">Govantes00</a>].  Expression is induced by iron limitation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1478458">Cotter92</a>] and H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> exposure [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11016692">Lindqvist00</a>], and is sensitive to the level of DNA supercoiling [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11238966">Bebbington01</a>]. <i>cydAB</i> is upregulated when exposed to nitric oxide and cytochrome <i>bd</i>-1 confers resistance to nitric oxide stress when compared to cytochrome <i>bo</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19109594">Mason09</a>].
<p>
GFP-tagged cytochrome <i>bd</i>-I concentrates in mobile localised areas of the inner membrane of <i>E. coli</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19019148">Lenn08</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21756872">Borisov11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32924537">Borisov21</a>]</comment>

<comment datatype="string">A cardiolipin is a diphosphatidylglycerol, composed of two <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=L-PHOSPHATIDATE" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=L-PHOSPHATIDATE''>1,2-Diacyl-<i>sn</i>-glycerol-3-phosphate</a>, often referred to as phosphatidate, is a class of compounds consisting of a <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=GLYCEROL''>glycerol</a> backbone, a (usually) saturated fatty acid bonded to carbon 1, a (usually) unsaturated fatty acid bonded to carbon 2, and a phosphate group esterified to carbon 3.">phosphatidate</a> molecules covalently linked to a molecule of glycerol at positions 1 and 3. It is an abundant anionic lipid in bacteria and in eukaryotes , where it is exclusively present in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
<p>
Cardiolipin was first isolated from beef heart [<a href="https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021925818726835">Pangborn42</a>], hence its name. 
<p>
Many enzymes involved in energy metabolism interact with cardiolipin. <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-7.1.1.9">EC 7.1.1.9, cytochrome-<em>c</em> oxidase</a>, also known as Complex IV, requires two associated cardiolipin molecules in order to maintain its full enzymatic function [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8389748">Robinson93</a>]. <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-7.1.1.8">EC 7.1.1.8, quinol&mdash;cytochrome-<em>c</em> reductase</a> (cytochrome <i>bc</i><sub>1</sub>, Complex III) also needs cardiolipin to maintain its quaternary structure and functional role [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10413476">Gomez99</a>]. <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-7.1.2.2">EC 7.1.2.2, H<small><sup>+</sup></small>-transporting two-sector ATPase</a> (Complex V) binds four molecules of cardiolipin [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2147180">Eble90</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">A cardiolipin is a diphosphatidylglycerol, composed of two <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=L-PHOSPHATIDATE" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=L-PHOSPHATIDATE''>1,2-Diacyl-<i>sn</i>-glycerol-3-phosphate</a>, often referred to as phosphatidate, is a class of compounds consisting of a <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=GLYCEROL''>glycerol</a> backbone, a (usually) saturated fatty acid bonded to carbon 1, a (usually) unsaturated fatty acid bonded to carbon 2, and a phosphate group esterified to carbon 3.">phosphatidate</a> molecules covalently linked to a molecule of glycerol at positions 1 and 3. It is an abundant anionic lipid in bacteria and in eukaryotes , where it is exclusively present in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
<p>
Cardiolipin was first isolated from beef heart [<a href="https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021925818726835">Pangborn42</a>], hence its name. 
<p>
Many enzymes involved in energy metabolism interact with cardiolipin. <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-7.1.1.9">EC 7.1.1.9, cytochrome-<em>c</em> oxidase</a>, also known as Complex IV, requires two associated cardiolipin molecules in order to maintain its full enzymatic function [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8389748">Robinson93</a>]. <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-7.1.1.8">EC 7.1.1.8, quinol&mdash;cytochrome-<em>c</em> reductase</a> (cytochrome <i>bc</i><sub>1</sub>, Complex III) also needs cardiolipin to maintain its quaternary structure and functional role [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10413476">Gomez99</a>]. <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-7.1.2.2">EC 7.1.2.2, H<small><sup>+</sup></small>-transporting two-sector ATPase</a> (Complex V) binds four molecules of cardiolipin [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2147180">Eble90</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">The ubiquinones are a group of lipid-soluble benzoquinones involved in electron transport. Their structures
have a variable length side chain, which consists of one to twelve mono-unsaturated
<I>trans</I>-isoprenoids units, with ten units being the most common in animals.
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-4932"><i>Saccharomyces cerevisiae</i></a> has 6 units, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-71421"><i>Haemophilus influenzae</i> Rd KW20</a> has 7, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-83333"><i>Escherichia coli</i> K-12</a> has 8, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1142"><i>Synechocystis</i></a>
has 9, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-9606"><i>Homo sapiens</i></a> has 10, and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1270"><i>Micrococcus luteus</i></a> has an 11 unit form [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16233343">Kawamukai02</a>].
<p>
The terms ubiquinone/ubiquinol refer to the oxidized/reduced forms, and are often used interchangeably.
The forms are readily interconvertable. 
<p>
Ubiquinone is also known as coenzyme Q, or just Q. The names are often followed by the number of the prenoid units in the side chain (e.g. Q-8), or the number of carbons in the chain. For example, the name Q-8 may be substituted with ubiiquinone(40). Since these carbons occur in repeating units of five, these number are multiples of 5.</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Ron Caspi received his PhD in Marine Microbiology in 1996 from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography in La Jolla, CA, under the guidance of Dr. Bradley Tebo and Dr. Margo Haygood. <comment datatype="string">The ubiquinones are a group of lipid-soluble benzoquinones involved in electron transport. Their structures
have a variable length side chain, which consists of one to twelve mono-unsaturated
<I>trans</I>-isoprenoids units, with ten units being the most common in animals.
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-4932"><i>Saccharomyces cerevisiae</i></a> has 6 units, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-71421"><i>Haemophilus influenzae</i> Rd KW20</a> has 7, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-83333"><i>Escherichia coli</i> K-12</a> has 8, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1142"><i>Synechocystis</i></a>
has 9, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-9606"><i>Homo sapiens</i></a> has 10, and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1270"><i>Micrococcus luteus</i></a> has an 11 unit form [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16233343">Kawamukai02</a>].
<p>
The terms ubiquinone/ubiquinol refer to the oxidized/reduced forms, and are often used interchangeably.
The forms are readily interconvertable. 
<p>
Ubiquinone is also known as coenzyme Q, or just Q. The names are often followed by the number of the prenoid units in the side chain (e.g. Q-8), or the number of carbons in the chain. For example, the name Q-8 may be substituted with ubiquinone(40). Since these carbons occur in repeating units of five, these number are multiples of 5.</comment>

<comment datatype='string'><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOYLCOA">Benzoyl-CoA</a> is a common intermediate in the anaerobic metabolism of aromatic compounds. The first step in the anaerobic degradation of benzoyl-CoA is its reduction to a cyclic dienoyl-CoA, a highly endergonic reaction.
<p>
Two types of enzymes are known to catalyze this transformation. Facultatively anaerobic microorganisms such as the phototrophic bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and the denitrifying bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a> employ <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.3.7.8">EC 1.3.7.8, benzoyl-CoA reductase</a>, also known as class I benzoyl-CoA reductase or class I BCR. These enzymes utilize ferredoxin as the electron donor, and couple the ring reduction to the hydrolysis of 2 molecules of ATP [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8575453">Boll95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9108255">Boll97</a>].
<p>
Obligately anaerobic bacteria such as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-28232"><i>Geobacter metallireducens</i></a> have a different type, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.3.1.M30">EC 1.3.1.M30, benzoyl-CoA reductase complex (NAD<small><sup>+</sup></small>, menaquinone, ferredoxin)</a> (referred to as "class II BCR"), which is a bifurcating enzyme that couples the endergonic aromatic ring reduction to the exergonic redox reaction of ferredoxin oxidation by NAD+, without ATP hydrolysis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21087381">Loffler11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24238333">Boll14</a>].
<p>
The class I enzyme of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a> is a heterotetramer composed of four different subunits. It contains three [4Fe-4S] clusters and catalyzes electron transfer from reduced ferredoxin to the substrate with concomitant ATP hydrolysis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8575453">Boll95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9108255">Boll97</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9746358">Breese98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10406950">Laempe99</a>, <a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bFEMSMicRev22-439%5d">Harwood99</a>]. Coupling with ATP hydrolysis is essential to overcome the high redox barrier for aromatic ring reduction.
<p>
Homologs of the enzyme are present in the genomes of all facultative anaerobes described so far [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16645310">Boll05</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype='string'><a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Ferredoxins">Ferredoxins</a> are present in all organisms, from bacteria and archaea to higher eukaryotes.
They are small and acidic proteins with prosthetic groups composed of iron and sulfur atoms, which are referred to as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers" title="Iron-sulfur clusters are cofators of <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=FeS-Proteins''>iron-sulfur proteins</a> and consist of a cluster of two to four iron atoms linked to sulfides, some of which are cysteine residues of the protein.&#10;&#10;Several cluster types have been described, including <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-23''>a [3Fe-3S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=3FE-4S''>a [3Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> and <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-7''>a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is relatively rare, and 3Fe/4Fe interconversion may occur with minimal protein reorganization. In another type of Fe-S cluster, known as <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD0-1098''>a Rieske [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, two of the 4 cysteine residues that are coordinated with the iron atoms in regular <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> are substituted by histidine residues. Although the clusters contain several iron atoms, each one usually transfers only one electron, so, for example, a protein with two [4Fe-4S] clusters will usually transfer two electrons.&#10;&#10;Small electron transfer proteins that contain only [2Fe-2S] or [4Fe-4S] clusters are called <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Ferredoxins''>ferredoxins</a>. When Fe-S clusters occur in larger (and sometimes membrane-bound) proteins together with other prosthetic groups and/or metal cofactors, the proteins are designated as complex Fe-S proteins. &#10;&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].">iron-sulfur clusters</a>. The ferredoxins function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential, and do not carry out classical enzyme functions. Ferredoxins characteristically transfer an electron
with a reduction potential E0' near -420mV (though the reduction potential of ferredoxins from some anaerobic microorganisms can be as low as -500mV [<a href="https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0013468616304133">Li16</a>] and as high as -340mV [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12610725">Thamer03</a>]).
<p>
Ferredoxins are classified into several groups according to the types and numbers of their Fe-S clusters. The <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=2Fe-2S-Ferredoxins">[2Fe-2S] ferredoxin</a> group consists of monomeric proteins containing a single <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>Iron-sulfur clusters</a> consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression regulation [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;In <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains.">a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. This group includes ferredoxins that transfer electrons in redox chains linked to hydroxylases and oxygenases in a wide range of organisms (from bacteria to mammals), and which includes plant and algal ferredoxins that function as electron carriers in photosynthesis. A related group contains <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Rieske-Type-Ferredoxins">a Rieske-type [2Fe-2S] ferredoxin</a>, where two of the cysteine groups are replaced by histidine residues.
<p>
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=4Fe-4S-Ferredoxins">[4Fe-4S] ferredoxins</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=3Fe-4S-Ferredoxins">[3Fe-4S] ferredoxins</a> are typically found in bacteria. They may differ in cluster type (3Fe or 4Fe), number of clusters (one or two), and length of polypeptide chain (up to over 100 residues), and include the relatively small dual cluster <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=2-4Fe-4S-Ferredoxins">2[4Fe-4S] ferredoxins</a> that were first isolated from anaerobic bacteria [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637">Park06</a>].
<p>
Even though each cluster contains more than one iron atom, each cluster can carry only one extra electron. Thus ferredoxins that contain a single cluster participate in single electron transfer reactions, while ferredoxins that carry two clusters can transfer two electrons simultaneously.
<p>
The structure given for this entry is that of a [2Fe-2S] ferredoxin, and is provided for illustration only.</comment>

<comment datatype='string'><a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Ferredoxins">Ferredoxins</a> are present in all organisms, from bacteria and archaea to higher eukaryotes.
They are small and acidic proteins with prosthetic groups composed of iron and sulfur atoms, which are referred to as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers" title="Iron-sulfur clusters are cofators of <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=FeS-Proteins''>iron-sulfur proteins</a> and consist of a cluster of two to four iron atoms linked to sulfides, some of which are cysteine residues of the protein.&#10;&#10;Several cluster types have been described, including <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-23''>a [3Fe-3S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=3FE-4S''>a [3Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> and <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-7''>a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is relatively rare, and 3Fe/4Fe interconversion may occur with minimal protein reorganization. In another type of Fe-S cluster, known as <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD0-1098''>a Rieske [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, two of the 4 cysteine residues that are coordinated with the iron atoms in regular <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> are substituted by histidine residues. Although the clusters contain several iron atoms, each one usually transfers only one electron, so, for example, a protein with two [4Fe-4S] clusters will usually transfer two electrons.&#10;&#10;Small electron transfer proteins that contain only [2Fe-2S] or [4Fe-4S] clusters are called <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Ferredoxins''>ferredoxins</a>. When Fe-S clusters occur in larger (and sometimes membrane-bound) proteins together with other prosthetic groups and/or metal cofactors, the proteins are designated as complex Fe-S proteins. &#10;&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].">iron-sulfur clusters</a>. The ferredoxins function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential, and do not carry out classical enzyme functions. Ferredoxins characteristically transfer an electron
with a reduction potential E0' near -420mV (though the reduction potential of ferredoxins from some anaerobic microorganisms can be as low as -500mV [<a href="https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0013468616304133">Li16</a>] and as high as -340mV [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12610725">Thamer03</a>]).
<p>
Ferredoxins are classified into several groups according to the types and numbers of their Fe-S clusters. The <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=2Fe-2S-Ferredoxins">[2Fe-2S] ferredoxin</a> group consists of monomeric proteins containing a single <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>Iron-sulfur clusters</a> consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression regulation [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;In <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains.">a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. This group includes ferredoxins that transfer electrons in redox chains linked to hydroxylases and oxygenases in a wide range of organisms (from bacteria to mammals), and which includes plant and algal ferredoxins that function as electron carriers in photosynthesis. A related group contains <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Rieske-Type-Ferredoxins">a Rieske-type [2Fe-2S] ferredoxin</a>, where two of the cysteine groups are replaced by histidine residues.
<p>
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=4Fe-4S-Ferredoxins">[4Fe-4S] ferredoxins</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=3Fe-4S-Ferredoxins">[3Fe-4S] ferredoxins</a> are typically found in bacteria. They may differ in cluster type (3Fe or 4Fe), number of clusters (one or two), and length of polypeptide chain (up to over 100 residues), and include the relatively small dual cluster <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=2-4Fe-4S-Ferredoxins">2[4Fe-4S] ferredoxins</a> that were first isolated from anaerobic bacteria [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637">Park06</a>].
<p>
Even though each cluster contains more than one iron atom, each cluster can carry only one extra electron. Thus ferredoxins that contain a single cluster participate in single electron transfer reactions, while ferredoxins that carry two clusters can transfer two electrons simultaneously.
<p>
The structure given for this entry is that of a [2Fe-2S] ferredoxin, and is provided for illustration only.</comment>

corresponding subunit of benzoyl-CoA reductase purified from <i>T. aromatica</i>, 
which is 38 kDa.  Furthermore, the deduced N terminal sequence of the badD gene product 
is 78% similar to the N-terminal amino acid sequence of the corresponding subunit of 
benzoyl-CoA reductase.  
<p>
The deduced amino acid sequences of BadD, E, F, and G are not similar to any other proteins
in genome databases, except for 2-hydroxyglutaryl-CoA dehydratase, an enzyme which catalyzes
a reversible dehydration of 2-hydroxyglutaryl-CoA to glutaconyl-CoA in glutamate fermentation in
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-905"><i>Acidaminococcus fermentans</i></a>  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177244">Egland97</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
Biodegradation of aromatic compounds is a common process in anoxic environments. The many natural and synthetic aromatic compounds found in the environment are usually degraded by anaerobic microorganisms into only few central intermediates, prior to ring cleavage [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9057820">Heider97</a>]. <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOYLCOA">Benzoyl-CoA</a> is the most important of these intermediates since a large number of compounds, including chloro-, nitro-, and aminobenzoates, aromatic hydrocarbons, and phenolic compounds, are initially converted to benzoyl-CoA prior to ring reduction and cleavage [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11282627">Elshahed01</a>].
<p>
The pathways for anaerobic benzoate and benzoyl-CoA degradation have been studied primarily in two microorganisms, the phototrophic, purple, nonsulfur bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and the nitrate-reducing bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a>.
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
Under anaerobic conditions, the phototrophic bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> can grow with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOATE">benzoate</a> as the sole carbon source and obtain energy from light via cyclic photophosphorylation. It is also capable of metabolizing the alicyclic acids <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-575">cyclohexane-1-carboxylate</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-21746">cyclohex-1-ene-1-carboxylate</a>, which then enter the benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway.
<p>
In both the phototroph <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and denitrifying bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a> anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation is initiated by reductive ring cleavage catalyzed by benzoyl-CoA reductase (see also <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=CENTBENZCOA-PWY">benzoyl-CoA degradation II (anaerobic)</a>).  This reaction is driven by the hydrolysis of 2 molecules of ATP and requires reduced ferrodoxin as an electron acceptor.  Whereas in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> the cyclic diene is further reduced to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-533">cyclohex-1-ene-1-carbonyl-CoA</a>, in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a> the cyclic diene is hydrated to<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=6-HYDROXYCYCLOHEX-1-ENE-1-CARBONYL-COA">6-hydroxycyclohex-1-ene-1-carbonyl-CoA</a>. The respective products are subsequently &beta;-oxidized to cyclic &beta;-oxo compounds, which in turn undergo hydrolytic ring cleavage to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-558">pimeloyl-CoA</a> in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=3-HYDROXYPIMELYL-COA">3-hydroxypimeloyl-CoA</a> in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a>.
<p>
These intermediates are further &beta;-oxidized via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTARYL-COA">glutaryl-CoA</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> in a segment of the pathway sometimes referred to as the "lower benzoyl-CoA pathway". The genes responsible for this segment up to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTARYL-COA">glutaryl-CoA</a> are contained in a single <i>pimFABCDE</i> cluster and constitute an operon. The gene predicted to encode <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.1.1.259">EC 1.1.1.259, 3-hydroxypimeloyl-CoA dehydrogenase</a>, <i>pimE</i>, appears to have a frameshift in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and may not encode a functional enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15758219">Harrison05</a>].
<p>
A <i>pim</i> operon deletion strain is still able to grow, albeit more slowly than the wild-type, on dicarboxylic acids and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOATE">benzoate</a>, indicating that the Pim enzymes are not the only <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> enzymes that can catalyze the degradation of these compounds [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15758219">Harrison05</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
Biodegradation of aromatic compounds is a common process in anoxic environments. The many natural and synthetic aromatic compounds found in the environment are usually degraded by anaerobic microorganisms into only few central intermediates, prior to ring cleavage [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9057820">Heider97</a>]. <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOYLCOA">Benzoyl-CoA</a> is the most important of these intermediates since a large number of compounds, including chloro-, nitro-, and aminobenzoates, aromatic hydrocarbons, and phenolic compounds, are initially converted to benzoyl-CoA prior to ring reduction and cleavage [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11282627">Elshahed01</a>].
<p>
The pathways for anaerobic benzoate and benzoyl-CoA degradation have been studied primarily in two microorganisms, the phototrophic, purple, nonsulfur bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and the nitrate-reducing bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a>.
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
Under anaerobic conditions, the phototrophic bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> can grow with <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOATE">benzoate</a> as the sole carbon source and obtain energy from light via cyclic photophosphorylation. It is also capable of metabolizing the alicyclic acids <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-575">cyclohexane-1-carboxylate</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-21746">cyclohex-1-ene-1-carboxylate</a>, which then enter the benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway.
<p>
In both the phototroph <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and denitrifying bacterium <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a> anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation is initiated by reductive ring cleavage catalyzed by benzoyl-CoA reductase (see also <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=CENTBENZCOA-PWY">benzoyl-CoA degradation II (anaerobic)</a>).  This reaction is driven by the hydrolysis of 2 molecules of ATP and requires reduced ferrodoxin as an electron acceptor.  Whereas in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> the cyclic diene is further reduced to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-533">cyclohex-1-ene-1-carbonyl-CoA</a>, in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a> the cyclic diene is hydrated to<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=6-HYDROXYCYCLOHEX-1-ENE-1-CARBONYL-COA">6-hydroxycyclohex-1-ene-1-carbonyl-CoA</a>. The respective products are subsequently &beta;-oxidized to cyclic &beta;-oxo compounds, which in turn undergo hydrolytic ring cleavage to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-558">pimeloyl-CoA</a> in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=3-HYDROXYPIMELYL-COA">3-hydroxypimeloyl-CoA</a> in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59405"><i>Thauera aromatica</i></a>.
<p>
These intermediates are further &beta;-oxidized via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTARYL-COA">glutaryl-CoA</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> in a segment of the pathway sometimes referred to as the "lower benzoyl-CoA pathway". The genes responsible for this segment up to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTARYL-COA">glutaryl-CoA</a> are contained in a single <i>pimFABCDE</i> cluster and constitute an operon. The gene predicted to encode <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-1.1.1.259">EC 1.1.1.259, 3-hydroxypimeloyl-CoA dehydrogenase</a>, <i>pimE</i>, appears to have a frameshift in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> and may not encode a functional enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15758219">Harrison05</a>].
<p>
A <i>pim</i> operon deletion strain is still able to grow, albeit more slowly than the wild-type, on dicarboxylic acids and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BENZOATE">benzoate</a>, indicating that the Pim enzymes are not the only <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-1076"><i>Rhodopseudomonas palustris</i></a> enzymes that can catalyze the degradation of these compounds [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15758219">Harrison05</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">PaaI belongs to the acyl-CoA thioesterase subfamily of the hotdog-fold superfamily of enzymes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15307895">Dillon04</a>].  Among the relevant phenylacetate degradation pathway intermediates, its primary substrate appears to be phenylacetyl-CoA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22398448">Teufel12</a>], although it was previously thought that its preferred substrates were ring-hydroxylated phenylacetyl-CoA thioesters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16464851">Song06</a>].  It may be involved in detoxification or salvage reactions for breakdown products of the unstable early intermediates of the phenylacetate degradation pathway [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22398448">Teufel12</a>].
<p>
A crystal structure of PaaI has been solved at 2 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16464851">Song06</a>].
<p>
A <i>paaI</i> mutant does not exhibit a defect in utilization of phenylacetate as a source of carbon [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12846838">Ismail03</a>].  PaaI activity is increased in cells grown on phenylacetate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22398448">Teufel12</a>].
<p>
PaaI: "<b>p</b>henyl<b>a</b>cetic <b>a</b>cid degradation" [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9748275">Ferrandez98</a>]</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-12258">paaA</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-12259">paaB</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-12260">paaC</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G-12261">paaE</a> genes of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-198931"><i>Pseudomonas</i> sp. <i>Y2</i></a> were cloned and expressed simultaneously in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>. PaaA alone was cloned as a maltose-binding protein (MBD) fusion protein. When purified by amylose resin chromatography, all proteins co-purified [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>].
<p>
The purified PaaABCE complex catalyzed a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-207">phenylacetyl-CoA</a>-induced and strictly oxygen-dependent NADPH consumption in a spectrophotometric assay, implying phenylacetyl-CoA oxygenase/reductase activity. The product was purified using reverse phase (RP)-HPLC, and mass spectrometry showed the incorporation of a single oxygen atom. <sup>18</sup>O studies showed that the oxygen atom originates from molecular oxygen, and <sup>13</sup>C-NMR analysis suggested that the product is <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2362">2-(1,2-epoxy-1,2-dihydrophenyl)acetyl-CoA</a>. Further proof was provided by derivatization of the epoxide.
Thus it was concluded that the PaaABCE complex functions as a <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-8168">ring 1,2-phenylacetyl-CoA epoxidase</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The ring 1,2-phenylacetyl-CoA epoxidase, comprised of the PaaA, PaaB, PaaC, and PaaE polypeptides, catalyzes the second step in the aerobic degradation of phenylacetate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21247899">Grishin11</a>].
<p>
Stable subcomplexes composed of PaaABC, PaaAC and PaaBC can be purified, but only the combination of the PaaABC complex together with PaaE has full activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21247899">Grishin11</a>].  Crystal structures of the PaaAC subcomplex alone and together with a variety of ligands have been solved [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20823522">Grishin10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21247899">Grishin11</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">PaaZ (oxepin-CoA hydrolase/3-oxo-5,6-dehydrosuberyl-CoA semialdehyde dehydrogenase) is a two-domain enzyme that catalyzes the two-step conversion of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2363">2-oxepin-2(3H)-ylideneacetyl-CoA</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2364">3-oxo-5,6-didehydrosuberyl-CoA</a> in phenylacetate catabolism.  The PaaZ protein consists of an N-terminal NADP-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase domain and a C-terminal MaoC-like (<i>R</i>)-specific enoyl-CoA hydratase domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21296885">Teufel11</a>].  The specific activity of the enzyme for the overall reaction is ~20 &micro;M min<sup>-1</sup> mg<sup>-1</sup> protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>].
<p>
3-oxo-5,6-dehydrosuberyl-CoA semialdehyde is a labile intermediate and can undergo spontaneous conversion to the dead-end product <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2558">2-hydroxycyclohepta-1,4,6-triene-1-carboxyl-CoA</a> through a Knoevenagel-type condensation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21296885">Teufel11</a>].  Avoiding this fate, 3-oxo-5,6-dehydrosuberyl-CoA is transferred between the two PaaZ active sites by electrostatic pivoting of the CoA moiety.  The positively charged residues K69, R613 and K636 appear to play a role in channeling [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31511507">Sathyanarayanan19</a>]
<p>
Cryo-EM structures of PaaZ show a tri-lobed structure consisting of three domain-swapped homodimers in which the C-terminal hydratase domains form the central core [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31511507">Sathyanarayanan19</a>].
<p>
PaaZ exhibits enoyl-CoA hydratase activity utilizing crotonyl-CoA as a substrate.  In a <i>fadB</i> mutant, PaaZ produces (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA for polyhydroxyalkanoate biosynthesis by exogenous <i>Pseudomonas</i> medium-chain-length polyhydroxyalkanoate synthase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12949091">Park03</a>]. 
<p>
A <i>paaZ</i> mutant exhibits a defect in utilization of phenylacetate as a source of carbon [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12846838">Ismail03</a>].  
<p>
PaaZ: "<b>p</b>henyl<b>a</b>cetic <b>a</b>cid degradation" [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9748275">Ferrandez98</a>]
<p>
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">IPI inferred from physical interaction

<br>
The assertion was inferred from a physical interaction such as
<ul>
    <li> 2-hybrid interactions
    <li> Co-purification
    <li> Co-immunoprecipitation
    <li> Ion/protein binding experiments
</ul><p class=ecocomment>
This code covers physical interactions between the gene product of
interest and another molecule (or ion, or complex). For functions such
as protein binding or nucleic acid binding, a binding assay is
simultaneously IPI and IDA; IDA is preferred because the assay
directly detects the binding. For both IPI and IGI, it would be good
practice to qualify them with the gene/protein/ion. 
</comment>
<common-name datatype="string">Inferred from physical interaction</common-name>
</Evidence-Code>

<comment datatype="string">IMP inferred from mutant phenotype.

<br>
The assertion was inferred from a mutant phenotype such as
<ul>
    <li> Any gene mutation/knockout
    <li> Overexpression/ectopic expression of wild-type or mutant genes
    <li> Anti-sense experiments
    <li> RNA interference experiments
    <li> Specific protein inhibitors
    <li> Complementation
</ul><p class=ecocomment>	
Comment: Inferences made from examining mutations or
abnormal levels of only the product(s) of the gene of interest are covered by code EV-IMP
(compare to code EV-IGI). Use this code for experiments that use antibodies 
or other specific inhibitors of RNA or protein activity, even though no
gene may be mutated (the rationale is that EV-IMP is used where an
abnormal situation prevails in a cell or organism).
</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string">The aerobic <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-12132">phenylacetate-coA ligase</a>, the enzyme catalyzing the first step in the aerobic degradation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PHENYLACETATE">phenylacetate</a>, has been purified from <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-59406"><i>Aromatoleum evansii</i></a> and characterized.
The enzyme was induced after aerobic growth in a chemically defined medium containing <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PHENYLACETATE">phenylacetate</a> or <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PHE">L-phenylalanine</a> as the sole carbon source. Enzymatic activity was detected very early in the exponential phase of growth.
<p>
The biochemical and molecular characteristics of this enzyme are very different from those of the isoenzyme catalyzing the same reaction under anaerobic conditions in the same bacterium [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10629172">ElSaid00</a>].
</comment>

The purified protein catalyzed the reversible conversion of enzymatically produced <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=TRANS-23-DEHYDROADIPYL-COA">(2<i>E</i>)-5-carboxy-2-pentenoyl-CoA</a> into <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=3-HYDROXYADIPYL-COA">(3S)-hydroxyadipyl-CoA</a>, as evidenced by mass spectrometry [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>].</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a> are dinucleotides containing one <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NIACINAMIDE">nicotinamide</a> base and one <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENINE">adenine</a> base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety.
<p>
These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cofactors" title="An enzyme cofactor is a non-protein chemical compound that is required by an enzyme for catalysis of a chemical reaction. Cofactors associate with inactive <i>apo</i>-enzymes, resulting in formation of active <i>holo</i>-enzymes.&#10;Unlike cosubstrates, the cofactors are restored to their original state at the end of the catalytic cycle and are thus not included in the reaction equation.&#10;&#10;Cofactors can be inorganic ions (e.g. Ca<sup>2+</sup>), inorganic molecules (e.g. <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>an iron-sulfur cluster</a>) or organic molecules (e.g. <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE''>pyridoxal 5'-phosphate</a>). Some compounds may act as cofactors for a particular enzyme and a cosubstrate for a different enzyme, depending on whether they are restored to their active state at the end of the reaction. &#10;Cofactors that are tightly bound to an enzyme have often been referred to as prosthetic groups. It should be noted that the degree of tightness required for this definition has not been defined, and that the same cofactor may bind differently to different enzymes, making this term imprecise. Thus, it is recommended not to use it. Organic cofactors that are loosely bound to the enzyme have been often referred to as coenzymes. However, that term is also imprecise, and it is recommended not to use it either.">cofactors</a>.  They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes".
<p>
The most common function of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADH">NADH</a>, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form.
<p>
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADPH">NADPH</a>, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a>, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a> is reduced by <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-84">photosystem I</a>. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY">pentose phosphate pathway (oxidative branch) I</a>).</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a> are dinucleotides containing one <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NIACINAMIDE">nicotinamide</a> base and one <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENINE">adenine</a> base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety.
<p>
These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cofactors" title="An enzyme cofactor is a non-protein chemical compound that is required by an enzyme for catalysis of a chemical reaction. Cofactors associate with inactive <i>apo</i>-enzymes, resulting in formation of active <i>holo</i>-enzymes.&#10;Unlike cosubstrates, the cofactors are restored to their original state at the end of the catalytic cycle and are thus not included in the reaction equation.&#10;&#10;Cofactors can be inorganic ions (e.g. Ca<sup>2+</sup>), inorganic molecules (e.g. <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>an iron-sulfur cluster</a>) or organic molecules (e.g. <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE''>pyridoxal 5'-phosphate</a>). Some compounds may act as cofactors for a particular enzyme and a cosubstrate for a different enzyme, depending on whether they are restored to their active state at the end of the reaction. &#10;Cofactors that are tightly bound to an enzyme have often been referred to as prosthetic groups. It should be noted that the degree of tightness required for this definition has not been defined, and that the same cofactor may bind differently to different enzymes, making this term imprecise. Thus, it is recommended not to use it. Organic cofactors that are loosely bound to the enzyme have been often referred to as coenzymes. However, that term is also imprecise, and it is recommended not to use it either.">cofactors</a>.  They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes".
<p>
The most common function of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADH">NADH</a>, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form.
<p>
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADPH">NADPH</a>, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a>, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a> is reduced by <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-84">photosystem I</a>. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY">pentose phosphate pathway (oxidative branch) I</a>).</comment>
