slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a> are dinucleotides containing one <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NIACINAMIDE">nicotinamide</a> base and one <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ADENINE">adenine</a> base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety.
<p>
These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Cofactors" title="An enzyme cofactor is a non-protein chemical compound that is required by an enzyme for catalysis of a chemical reaction. Cofactors associate with inactive <i>apo</i>-enzymes, resulting in formation of active <i>holo</i>-enzymes.&#10;Unlike cosubstrates, the cofactors are restored to their original state at the end of the catalytic cycle and are thus not included in the reaction equation.&#10;&#10;Cofactors can be inorganic ions (e.g. Ca<sup>2+</sup>), inorganic molecules (e.g. <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>an iron-sulfur cluster</a>) or organic molecules (e.g. <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE''>pyridoxal 5'-phosphate</a>). Some compounds may act as cofactors for a particular enzyme and a cosubstrate for a different enzyme, depending on whether they are restored to their active state at the end of the reaction. &#10;Cofactors that are tightly bound to an enzyme have often been referred to as prosthetic groups. It should be noted that the degree of tightness required for this definition has not been defined, and that the same cofactor may bind differently to different enzymes, making this term imprecise. Thus, it is recommended not to use it. Organic cofactors that are loosely bound to the enzyme have been often referred to as coenzymes. However, that term is also imprecise, and it is recommended not to use it either.">cofactors</a>.  They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes".
<p>
The most common function of  <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NAD">NAD<sup>+</sup></a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADH">NADH</a>, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form.
<p>
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADPH">NADPH</a>, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a>, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=NADP">NADP<sup>+</sup></a> is reduced by <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-84">photosystem I</a>. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY">pentose phosphate pathway (oxidative branch) I</a>).</comment>

slots.name: comment
slots.xml:
<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PHENYLACETATE">Phenylacetate</a> is a major intermediate in bacterial degradation of many aromatic compounds [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11260461">Luengo01</a>]. Microbes can oxidize phenylacetate under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see also <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-1341">phenylacetate degradation II (anaerobic)</a>), and the first step in both pathways is the same - the activition of phenylacetate to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-207">phenylacetyl-CoA</a> by a <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=MONOMER-12132">phenylacetate-CoA ligase</a>.
<p>
Despite the fact that the existence of an aerobic pathway was reported back in 1955 [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bKunita55%5d">Kunita55</a>], the exact chemistry, which is unusual for an aerobic pathway, was solved only in 2010 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>]. All of the pathway's intermediates remain in the form of CoA-thioesters, a characteristic typical of anaerobic degradation pathways. 
<p>
De-aromatization of the ring is achieved by activation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-207">phenylacetyl-CoA</a> to a <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2362">2-(1,2-epoxy-1,2-dihydrophenyl)acetyl-CoA</a>, catalyzed by <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX-8168">ring 1,2-phenylacetyl-CoA epoxidase</a>, a multicomponent oxygenase. The reactive non-aromatic epoxide is then isomerized to a seven-member <i>o</i>-heterocyclic enol ether, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2363">2-oxepin-2(3H)-ylideneacetyl-CoA</a>, and the ring is cleaved. The rest of the pathway consists of &beta;-oxidation steps leading to formation of the TCA cycle intermediates <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETYL-COA">acetyl-CoA</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=SUC-COA">succinyl-CoA</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17259607">Nogales07</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660314">Teufel10</a>].</comment>
